title: Jesuit astronomers at the Qing court
summary: From 1644 the new Qing court adopted the Western calendar method, and Jesuit Johann Adam Schall von Bell became the first regular director of the Astronomical Bureau in Beijing. After a calendar dispute, his successor Ferdinand Verbiest was put in charge of the Bureau's affairs in 1669, and Jesuits kept directing observation and calendar work.

as_recorded.value: 1644, the xifa (Western rule) accepted as the only authorized one; Schall first regular Director of the Astronomical Bureau
12 July 1669, the Emperor placed Verbiest in charge of the Bureau's affairs; he held the office until his death in 1688
1645, calendar texts reissued as the Calendar Compendium following the New Western Method

when.display: 1644–1688 (Schall von Bell to Verbiest; Jesuit service at the Bureau continued after)

where.historical_name: Beijing, capital of the Qing empire (seat of the Imperial Board of Astronomy)

importance.justification: Placed European mathematical astronomy at the centre of Qing calendar-making for generations and opened a channel of scientific exchange between Europe and China.

beats.caption: As the Qing dynasty began, the Western calendar method was authorized and Schall von Bell became first regular director of the Astronomical Bureau.
Calendar texts were reissued as the Calendar Compendium following the New Western Method, one of the dynasty's first initiatives.
After the calendar dispute, Ferdinand Verbiest replaced Yang Guangxian and was placed in charge of the Bureau's affairs.

reviewer_note: The id says 1736 but no opened page ties the record to that year; 1644 is the sourced start and the id was kept as instructed. The end year 1688 is Verbiest's death; other accounts have Jesuits holding the post for about 150 years but no opened page gave an end date. The pin is the Beijing Ancient Observatory, used as a stand-in for the Bureau's seat in Beijing (not stated in an opened source). Schall's exact appointment year is not given on the opened pages.
